7 Proof of Theorem 3.2

Lemma 7.1 (Lemma 1 in Kaufmann et al. [2016])

Let μ∈ℋ\mu\in\mathcal{H} and λ∈Alt⁡(μ)\lambda\in\mathrm{Alt}(\mu) denote two instances of the LLM policy optimization problem. For any experiment design, every stopping time τ\tau and event ℰ\mathcal{E}, it holds that

∑(i,j)∈𝒮𝔼μ​[Ni​j​(τ)]​d​(μ⁡(i,j),λ⁡(i,j))≥kl​(ℙμ​(ℰ),ℙλ​(ℰ)),\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[N_{ij}(\tau)]d(\mu(i,j),\lambda(i,j))\geq\text{kl}(\mathbb{P}_{\mu}(\mathcal{E}),\mathbb{P}_{\lambda}(\mathcal{E})),

where Ni​j​(τ)N_{ij}(\tau) is the number of samples from policy pair (i,j)(i,j) up to time step τ\tau, and kl​(x,y)\text{kl}(x,y) is defined as

kl​(x,y):=x​log⁡(xy)+(1−x)​log⁡(1−x1−y).\text{kl}(x,y):=x\log\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)+(1-x)\log\left(\frac{1-x}{1-y}\right).

Fix δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2) and an instance μ∈ℋ\mu\in\mathcal{H}. Consider any δ\delta-PAC adaptive simulation experiment with stopping time τ\tau and final decision i^τ\hat{i}_{\tau}. By the δ\delta-PAC requirement, for all μ∈ℋ\mu\in\mathcal{H},

ℙμ​(i^τ=i⋆​(μ))≥1−δ,equivalentlyℙμ​(i^τ≠i⋆​(μ))≤δ.\mathbb{P}_{\mu}(\hat{i}_{\tau}=i^{\star}(\mu))\geq 1-\delta,\hskip 17.00024pt\text{equivalently}\hskip 17.00024pt\mathbb{P}_{\mu}(\hat{i}_{\tau}\neq i^{\star}(\mu))\leq\delta. (10)

Moreover, for any alternative instance λ∈Alt⁡(μ)\lambda\in\mathrm{Alt}(\mu) (so that i⋆​(λ)≠i⋆​(μ)i^{\star}(\lambda)\neq i^{\star}(\mu)), the same decision rule must satisfy

ℙλ​(i^τ=i⋆​(λ))≥1−δ⇒ℙλ​(i^τ≠i⋆​(μ))≥1−δ.\mathbb{P}_{\lambda}(\hat{i}_{\tau}=i^{\star}(\lambda))\geq 1-\delta\hskip 8.50012pt\Rightarrow\hskip 8.50012pt\mathbb{P}_{\lambda}(\hat{i}_{\tau}\neq i^{\star}(\mu))\geq 1-\delta. (11)

Define the error event

ℰ:={i^τ≠i⋆(μ)}.\mathcal{E}:=\{\hat{i}_{\tau}\neq i^{\star}(\mu)\}.

Then (10)–(11) give

ℙμ​(ℰ)≤δ,ℙλ​(ℰ)≥1−δ∀λ∈Alt⁡(μ).\mathbb{P}_{\mu}(\mathcal{E})\leq\delta,\hskip 17.00024pt\mathbb{P}_{\lambda}(\mathcal{E})\geq 1-\delta\hskip 17.00024pt\forall\lambda\in\mathrm{Alt}(\mu).

Applying Lemma 7.1 yields: for every λ∈Alt⁡(μ)\lambda\in\mathrm{Alt}(\mu),

∑(i,j)∈𝒮𝔼μ​[Ni​j​(τ)]​d​(μ⁡(i,j),λ⁡(i,j))≥kl​(ℙμ​(ℰ),ℙλ​(ℰ))≥kl​(δ,1−δ),\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\big[N_{ij}(\tau)\big]\;d\big(\mu(i,j),\lambda(i,j)\big)\;\geq\;\text{kl}\big(\mathbb{P}_{\mu}(\mathcal{E}),\mathbb{P}_{\lambda}(\mathcal{E})\big)\;\geq\;\text{kl}(\delta,1-\delta), (12)

where the last inequality follows since δ<1/2\delta<1/2, for x<yx<y the binary relative entropy kl​(x,y)\text{kl}(x,y) is decreasing in xx and increasing in yy.

Now combine the inequalities over all alternatives λ∈Alt⁡(μ)\lambda\in\mathrm{Alt}(\mu):

kl​(δ,1−δ)\displaystyle\text{kl}(\delta,1-\delta) ≤infλ∈Alt⁡(μ)∑(i,j)∈𝒮𝔼μ​[Ni​j​(τ)]​d​(μ⁡(i,j),λ⁡(i,j))\displaystyle\leq\inf_{\lambda\in\mathrm{Alt}(\mu)}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\big[N_{ij}(\tau)\big]\;d\big(\mu(i,j),\lambda(i,j)\big)
=infλ∈Alt⁡(μ)𝔼μ​[τ]​∑(i,j)∈𝒮𝔼μ​[Ni​j​(τ)]𝔼μ​[τ]​d​(μ⁡(i,j),λ⁡(i,j))\displaystyle=\inf_{\lambda\in\mathrm{Alt}(\mu)}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\tau]\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}}\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\big[N_{ij}(\tau)\big]}{\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\tau]}\;d\big(\mu(i,j),\lambda(i,j)\big)
≤𝔼μ​[τ]​supω∈Ωinfλ∈Alt⁡(μ)∑(i,j)∈𝒮ωi​j​d​(μ⁡(i,j),λ⁡(i,j)),\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\tau]\;\sup_{\omega\in\Omega}\inf_{\lambda\in\mathrm{Alt}(\mu)}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}}\omega_{ij}\;d\big(\mu(i,j),\lambda(i,j)\big), (13)

where in the second line we used 𝔼μ​[τ]=∑(i,j)∈𝒮𝔼μ​[Ni​j​(τ)]\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\tau]=\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[N_{ij}(\tau)], and in the last line we introduced

ωi​j:=𝔼μ​[Ni​j​(τ)]𝔼μ​[τ],so thatω∈Ω:={ω≥0:∑i<jωi​j=1}.\omega_{ij}:=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[N_{ij}(\tau)]}{\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\tau]},\hskip 17.00024pt\text{so that}\hskip 17.00024pt\omega\in\Omega:=\Big\{\omega\geq 0:\sum_{i<j}\omega_{ij}=1\Big\}.

Rearranging (13) gives

𝔼μ​[τ]≥kl​(δ,1−δ)supω∈Ωinfλ∈Alt⁡(μ)∑(i,j)∈𝒮ωi​j​d​(μ⁡(i,j),λ⁡(i,j))=𝒯⋆​(μ)​kl​(δ,1−δ),\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\tau]\;\geq\;\frac{\text{kl}(\delta,1-\delta)}{\sup_{\omega\in\Omega}\inf_{\lambda\in\mathrm{Alt}(\mu)}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}}\omega_{ij}d(\mu(i,j),\lambda(i,j))}\;=\;\mathcal{T}^{\star}(\mu)\,\text{kl}(\delta,1-\delta), (14)

where 𝒯⋆​(μ)\mathcal{T}^{\star}(\mu) is defined by (2). This proves the first claim.

Finally, since kl​(δ,1−δ)∼log⁡(1/δ)\text{kl}(\delta,1-\delta)\sim\log(1/\delta) as δ→0\delta\to 0, dividing (14) by log⁡(1/δ)\log(1/\delta) and taking lim infδ→0\liminf_{\delta\to 0} yields

lim infδ→0𝔼μ​[τ]log⁡(1/δ)≥𝒯⋆​(μ),\liminf_{\delta\to 0}\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\tau]}{\log(1/\delta)}\geq\mathcal{T}^{\star}(\mu),

which completes the proof. □\square ∎

8 Proof of Corollary 3.3

For each i∈[K]i\in[K], define the dominance region

𝒞i:={λ∈ℋ:minj≠i⁡λ⁡(i,j)>12}.\mathcal{C}_{i}:=\Big\{\lambda\in\mathcal{H}:\ \min_{j\neq i}\lambda(i,j)>\tfrac{1}{2}\Big\}. (15)

Then i⋆​(λ)=ii^{\star}(\lambda)=i if and only if λ∈𝒞i\lambda\in\mathcal{C}_{i}. In particular,

Alt⁡(μ)={λ∈ℋ:i⋆​(λ)≠i⋆​(μ)}=⋃i≠i⋆​(μ)𝒞i.\mathrm{Alt}(\mu)=\{\lambda\in\mathcal{H}:i^{\star}(\lambda)\neq i^{\star}(\mu)\}=\bigcup_{i\neq i^{\star}(\mu)}\mathcal{C}_{i}. (16)

The optimization problem in (2) is furthermore equivalent to

𝒯⋆(μ)−1=maxω∈Ωinfλ∈Alt⁡(μ)∑(i,j)∈𝒮ωi​jd(μ(i,j),λ(i,j))=maxω∈Ωmini≠i⋆​(μ)infλ∈𝒞i∑(i,j)∈𝒮ωi​jd(μ(i,j),λ(i,j)).\mathcal{T}^{\star}(\mu)^{-1}=\max_{\omega\in\Omega}\inf_{\lambda\in\mathrm{Alt}(\mu)}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}}\omega_{ij}d(\mu(i,j),\lambda(i,j))=\max_{\omega\in\Omega}\min_{i\neq i^{\star}(\mu)}\inf_{\lambda\in\mathcal{C}_{i}}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}}\omega_{ij}d(\mu(i,j),\lambda(i,j)).

Fix i≠i⋆​(μ)i\neq i^{\star}(\mu) and ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega. Since the constraints defining 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} only involve comparisons between ii and other policies, the inner objective decomposes, and only terms involving ii may change. Define

Fi​(ω,λ):=∑j<iωj​i​d​(μ⁡(j,i),λ⁡(j,i))+∑h>iωi​h​d​(μ⁡(i,h),λ⁡(i,h)).F_{i}(\omega,\lambda):=\sum_{j<i}\omega_{ji}\,d\big(\mu(j,i),\lambda(j,i)\big)+\sum_{h>i}\omega_{ih}\,d\big(\mu(i,h),\lambda(i,h)\big). (17)

Then

infλ∈𝒞i∑i<jωi​j​d​(μ⁡(i,j),λ⁡(i,j))=infλ∈𝒞iFi​(ω,λ).\inf_{\lambda\in\mathcal{C}_{i}}\sum_{i<j}\omega_{ij}d(\mu(i,j),\lambda(i,j))=\inf_{\lambda\in\mathcal{C}_{i}}F_{i}(\omega,\lambda). (18)

We next characterize the infimum over 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i}. For λ∈𝒞i\lambda\in\mathcal{C}_{i}, we require λ⁡(i,j)>12\lambda(i,j)>\tfrac{1}{2} for all j≠ij\neq i. Thus, for every j<ij<i with μ⁡(j,i)>12\mu(j,i)>\tfrac{1}{2}, the value λ⁡(j,i)\lambda(j,i) must be moved from above 12\tfrac{1}{2} to below 12\tfrac{1}{2}; similarly, for every h>ih>i with μ⁡(i,h)<12\mu(i,h)<\tfrac{1}{2}, the value λ⁡(i,h)\lambda(i,h) must be moved from below 12\tfrac{1}{2} to above 12\tfrac{1}{2}.

Note that if p<12p<\tfrac{1}{2}, then

infq>12d⁡(p,q)=d⁡(p,12),\inf_{q>\tfrac{1}{2}}d(p,q)=d\left(p,\tfrac{1}{2}\right), (19)

and the infimum is approached by q↓12q\downarrow\tfrac{1}{2}. Likewise, if p>12p>\tfrac{1}{2}, then

infq<12d⁡(p,q)=d⁡(p,12),\inf_{q<\tfrac{1}{2}}d(p,q)=d\left(p,\tfrac{1}{2}\right),

and the infimum is approached by q↑12q\uparrow\tfrac{1}{2}.

Applying these facts coordinate-wise, an infimizing sequence over 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} is obtained by setting

λ⁡(j,i)↑12​for all ​j∈ℐ1​(i),λ⁡(i,h)↓12​for all ​h∈ℐ2​(i),\lambda(j,i)\uparrow\tfrac{1}{2}\hskip 8.50012pt\text{for all }j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}(i),\hskip 17.00024pt\lambda(i,h)\downarrow\tfrac{1}{2}\hskip 8.50012pt\text{for all }h\in\mathcal{I}_{2}(i),

while keeping all other pairs unchanged. Consequently,

𝒯⋆​(μ)−1=maxω∈Ω⁡min⁡∑j∈ℐ1​(i)i≠i⋆​(μ)⁡ωj​i​d​(μ⁡(j,i),12)+∑h∈ℐ2​(i)ωi​h​d​(μ⁡(i,h),12),\mathcal{T}^{\star}(\mu)^{-1}=\max_{\omega\in\Omega}\min_{i\neq i^{\star}(\mu)}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}(i)}\omega_{ji}d\left(\mu(j,i),\frac{1}{2}\right)+\sum_{h\in\mathcal{I}_{2}(i)}\omega_{ih}d\left(\mu(i,h),\frac{1}{2}\right), (20)

where the set ℐ1​(i)={j∈[K]:j⁡<i,μ⁡(j,i)>​12}\mathcal{I}_{1}(i)=\{j\in[K]:j<i,\mu(j,i)>\frac{1}{2}\}, and ℐ2(i)={h∈[K]:i<h,μ(i,h)<12}\mathcal{I}_{2}(i)=\{h\in[K]:i<h,\mu(i,h)<\frac{1}{2}\}.

Consider the epigraph formulation (21):

max⁡ν\displaystyle\max\hskip 8.50012pt\nu (21)
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} ∑j∈ℐ1​(i)ωj​id(μ(j,i),12)+∑h∈ℐ2​(i)ωi​hd(μ(i,h),12)≥ν,∀i≠i⋆(μ),(ρi)\displaystyle\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}(i)}\omega_{ji}d\left(\mu(j,i),\frac{1}{2}\right)+\sum_{h\in\mathcal{I}_{2}(i)}\omega_{ih}d\left(\mu(i,h),\frac{1}{2}\right)\geq\nu,\hskip 8.50012pt\forall i\neq i^{\star}(\mu),\hskip 8.50012pt(\rho_{i})
∑i<jωi​j=1,(γ)\displaystyle\sum_{i<j}\omega_{ij}=1,\hskip 8.50012pt(\gamma)
ωi​j≥0,∀i<j,(ξi​j).\displaystyle\omega_{ij}\geq 0,\hskip 8.50012pt\forall i<j,\hskip 8.50012pt(\xi_{ij}).

Let (ν,ω)(\nu,\omega) be a primal optimal solution and (ρ,γ,ξ)(\rho,\gamma,\xi) be KKT multipliers associated with the Lagrangian

ℒ⁡(ν,ω,ρ,γ,ξ)=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\nu,\omega,\rho,\gamma,\xi)= ν+∑i≠i⋆​(μ)ρi​(∑j∈ℐ1​(i)ωj​i​d​(μ⁡(j,i),12)+∑h∈ℐ2​(i)ωi​h​d​(μ⁡(i,h),12)−ν)\displaystyle\nu+\sum_{i\neq i^{\star}(\mu)}\rho_{i}\left(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}(i)}\omega_{ji}d\left(\mu(j,i),\tfrac{1}{2}\right)+\sum_{h\in\mathcal{I}_{2}(i)}\omega_{ih}d\left(\mu(i,h),\tfrac{1}{2}\right)-\nu\right) (22)
−γ⁡(∑i<jωi​j−1)+∑i<jξi​j​ωi​j,\displaystyle-\gamma\left(\sum_{i<j}\omega_{ij}-1\right)+\sum_{i<j}\xi_{ij}\omega_{ij},

where ρi≥0\rho_{i}\geq 0 and ξi​j≥0\xi_{ij}\geq 0.

The KKT conditions include:

  • •

    Stationarity with respect to ν\nu:

    ∑i≠i⋆​(μ)ρi=1,\sum_{i\neq i^{\star}(\mu)}\rho_{i}=1, (23)
  • •

    Stationarity with respect to ωi​j\omega_{ij} with i<ji<j:

    ρi​d​(μ⁡(i,j),12)​𝕀​(μ⁡(i,j)<12)+ρj​d​(μ⁡(i,j),12)​𝕀​(μ⁡(i,j)>12)+ξi​j=γ\rho_{i}d\left(\mu(i,j),\frac{1}{2}\right)\mathbb{I}\left(\mu(i,j)<\frac{1}{2}\right)+\rho_{j}d\left(\mu(i,j),\frac{1}{2}\right)\mathbb{I}\left(\mu(i,j)>\frac{1}{2}\right)+\xi_{ij}=\gamma (24)
  • •

    Complementary Slackness:

    ρi​(∑j∈ℐ1​(i)ωj​i​d​(μ⁡(j,i),12)+∑h∈ℐ2​(i)ωi​h​d​(μ⁡(i,h),12)−ν)=0,∀i≠i⋆​(μ),\rho_{i}\left(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}(i)}\omega_{ji}d\left(\mu(j,i),\frac{1}{2}\right)+\sum_{h\in\mathcal{I}_{2}(i)}\omega_{ih}d\left(\mu(i,h),\frac{1}{2}\right)-\nu\right)=0,\hskip 8.50012pt\forall i\neq i^{\star}(\mu), (25)

    and

    ξi​j​ωi​j=0,∀i<j.\xi_{ij}\omega_{ij}=0,\hskip 8.50012pt\forall i<j. (26)

Since d⁡(⋅,⋅)≥0d(\cdot,\cdot)\geq 0 and ωi​j≥0\omega_{ij}\geq 0, the left-hand side of each inequality constraint in (21) is nonnegative. Therefore, for any ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega, the pair (ν,ω)=(0,ω)(\nu,\omega)=(0,\omega) is feasible. Hence the optimal value of (21) is at least 00, that is, ν⋆≥0\nu^{\star}\geq 0.

We next show that the optimal value is strictly positive. Fix any i≠i⋆​(μ)i\neq i^{\star}(\mu). Since μ∈ℋ\mu\in\mathcal{H} admits a unique optimal policy i⋆​(μ)i^{\star}(\mu), policy ii must be defeated by at least one other policy. Equivalently,

ℐ1​(i)∪ℐ2​(i)≠∅.\mathcal{I}_{1}(i)\cup\mathcal{I}_{2}(i)\neq\varnothing.

Hence there exists at least one comparison involving ii whose associated divergence term is strictly positive, that is,

d⁡(μ⁡(j,i),12)>0​for some ​j∈ℐ1​(i),d\left(\mu(j,i),\tfrac{1}{2}\right)>0\hskip 8.50012pt\text{for some }j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}(i),

or

d⁡(μ⁡(i,h),12)>0​for some ​h∈ℐ2​(i).d\left(\mu(i,h),\tfrac{1}{2}\right)>0\hskip 8.50012pt\text{for some }h\in\mathcal{I}_{2}(i).

Now choose any ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega with full support, i.e., ωi​j>0\omega_{ij}>0 for all i<ji<j. Then, for every i≠i⋆​(μ)i\neq i^{\star}(\mu), the left-hand side of the ii-th constraint in (21) is strictly positive. Since there are only finitely many such ii, their minimum is also strictly positive. Therefore, there exists some ν¯>0\bar{\nu}>0 such that (ν¯,ω)(\bar{\nu},\omega) is feasible for (21). It follows that the optimal value satisfies ν⋆>0.\nu^{\star}>0.

According to (23), there exists some p≠i⋆​(μ)p\neq i^{\star}(\mu) such that ρp>0\rho_{p}>0. Since pp is suboptimal under μ\mu, it must be defeated by at least one other policy. Equivalently, either there exists k<pk<p such that μ⁡(k,p)>12\mu(k,p)>\tfrac{1}{2}, or there exists k>pk>p such that μ⁡(p,k)<12\mu(p,k)<\tfrac{1}{2}. In either case, the corresponding divergence term is strictly positive. If k<pk<p, then applying (24) to the pair (k,p)(k,p) gives

γ=ρp​d​(μ⁡(k,p),12)+ξk​p.\gamma=\rho_{p}\,d\left(\mu(k,p),\tfrac{1}{2}\right)+\xi_{kp}.

Since ρp>0\rho_{p}>0, d⁡(μ⁡(k,p),12)>0d(\mu(k,p),\tfrac{1}{2})>0, and ξk​p≥0\xi_{kp}\geq 0, it follows that γ>0\gamma>0. If instead k>pk>p, then applying (24) to the pair (p,k)(p,k) yields

γ=ρp​d​(μ⁡(p,k),12)+ξp​k.\gamma=\rho_{p}\,d\left(\mu(p,k),\tfrac{1}{2}\right)+\xi_{pk}.

Again, since ρp>0\rho_{p}>0, d⁡(μ⁡(p,k),12)>0d(\mu(p,k),\tfrac{1}{2})>0, and ξp​k≥0\xi_{pk}\geq 0, we obtain γ>0\gamma>0. Hence, γ>0\gamma>0.

Suppose, for contradiction, that there exists i≠i⋆​(μ)i\neq i^{\star}(\mu) such that ρi=0\rho_{i}=0. First, consider any h∈ℐ2​(i)h\in\mathcal{I}_{2}(i). Then i<hi<h and μ⁡(i,h)<12\mu(i,h)<\tfrac{1}{2}. Applying (24) to the pair (i,h)(i,h) gives

ρi​d​(μ⁡(i,h),12)−γ+ξi​h=0.\rho_{i}d\left(\mu(i,h),\tfrac{1}{2}\right)-\gamma+\xi_{ih}=0.

Since ρi=0\rho_{i}=0 and γ>0\gamma>0, we obtain ξi​h=γ>0\xi_{ih}=\gamma>0. By complementary slackness (26), it follows that

ωi​h=0,∀h∈ℐ2​(i).\omega_{ih}=0,\hskip 17.00024pt\forall h\in\mathcal{I}_{2}(i).

Next, consider any j∈ℐ1​(i)j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}(i). Then j<ij<i and μ⁡(j,i)>12\mu(j,i)>\tfrac{1}{2}. Applying (24) to the pair (j,i)(j,i) yields

ρi​d​(μ⁡(j,i),12)−γ+ξj​i=0.\rho_{i}d\left(\mu(j,i),\tfrac{1}{2}\right)-\gamma+\xi_{ji}=0.

Again, since ρi=0\rho_{i}=0 and γ>0\gamma>0, we have ξj​i=γ>0\xi_{ji}=\gamma>0, and thus ωj​i=0\omega_{ji}=0 by (26). Therefore,

ωj​i=0,∀j∈ℐ1​(i).\omega_{ji}=0,\hskip 17.00024pt\forall j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}(i).

Consequently, every term in the ii-th constraint of (21) vanishes, so

∑j∈ℐ1​(i)ωj​i​d​(μ⁡(j,i),12)+∑h∈ℐ2​(i)ωi​h​d​(μ⁡(i,h),12)=0.\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}(i)}\omega_{ji}d\left(\mu(j,i),\tfrac{1}{2}\right)+\sum_{h\in\mathcal{I}_{2}(i)}\omega_{ih}d\left(\mu(i,h),\tfrac{1}{2}\right)=0.

Since (ν,ω)(\nu,\omega) is primal feasible and (ν,ω)(\nu,\omega) is optimal, we have ν=ν⋆\nu=\nu^{\star}. Therefore, the ii-th constraint implies 0≥ν=ν⋆0\geq\nu=\nu^{\star}, contradicting ν⋆>0\nu^{\star}>0. Hence ρi>0\rho_{i}>0 for all i≠i⋆​(μ)i\neq i^{\star}(\mu).

Since ρi>0\rho_{i}>0 for all i≠i⋆​(μ)i\neq i^{\star}(\mu), complementary slackness (25) implies

∑j∈ℐ1​(i)ωj​i​d​(μ⁡(j,i),12)+∑h∈ℐ2​(i)ωi​h​d​(μ⁡(i,h),12)=ν,∀i≠i⋆​(μ).\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}(i)}\omega_{ji}d\left(\mu(j,i),\tfrac{1}{2}\right)+\sum_{h\in\mathcal{I}_{2}(i)}\omega_{ih}d\left(\mu(i,h),\tfrac{1}{2}\right)=\nu,\hskip 8.50012pt\forall i\neq i^{\star}(\mu). (27)

Fix i≠i⋆​(μ)i\neq i^{\star}(\mu). If ωj​i>0\omega_{ji}>0 for some j∈ℐ1​(i)j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}(i), then (26) gives ξj​i=0\xi_{ji}=0, and since μ⁡(j,i)>12\mu(j,i)>\tfrac{1}{2}, (24) yields

If ωi​h>0\omega_{ih}>0 for some h∈ℐ2​(i)h\in\mathcal{I}_{2}(i), then (26) gives ξi​h=0\xi_{ih}=0, and since μ⁡(i,h)<12\mu(i,h)<\tfrac{1}{2}, (24) yields

Hence, within the ii-th tight constraint, all comparisons carrying positive mass must have the same divergence value.

Now let

di⋆:=max⁡{maxj∈ℐ1​(i)⁡d⁡(μ⁡(j,i),12),maxh∈ℐ2​(i)⁡d⁡(μ⁡(i,h),12)},d_{i}^{\star}:=\max\Big\{\max_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}(i)}d\left(\mu(j,i),\tfrac{1}{2}\right),\ \max_{h\in\mathcal{I}_{2}(i)}d\left(\mu(i,h),\tfrac{1}{2}\right)\Big\},

and let j~​(i)∈ℐ1​(i)∪ℐ2​(i)\tilde{j}(i)\in\mathcal{I}_{1}(i)\cup\mathcal{I}_{2}(i) be any maximizer achieving di⋆d_{i}^{\star}. Since each comparison pair appears in exactly one suboptimal-policy constraint, for each i≠i⋆​(μ)i\neq i^{\star}(\mu) we may redistribute all mass assigned to the ii-th constraint onto the single comparison associated with j~​(i)\tilde{j}(i), without affecting any other constraint or the total mass constraint. Moreover, any mass assigned to pairs outside

τ≲max⁡{t0,tε′,tid,c11−ε​𝒰⋆​(μ)​log⁡1δ}.\tau\lesssim\max\left\{t_{0},t_{\varepsilon}^{\prime},t_{\rm id},\,\frac{c_{1}}{1-\varepsilon}\mathcal{U}^{\star}(\mu)\log\frac{1}{\delta}\right\}.

Hence, on ℰ\mathcal{E},

lim supδ→0τlog⁡(1/δ)≲c11−ε​𝒰⋆​(μ).\limsup_{\delta\rightarrow 0}\frac{\tau}{\log(1/\delta)}\lesssim\frac{c_{1}}{1-\varepsilon}\mathcal{U}^{\star}(\mu).

Letting ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0, we obtain

lim supδ→0τlog⁡(1/δ)≲𝒰⋆​(μ)on ​ℰ.\limsup_{\delta\rightarrow 0}\frac{\tau}{\log(1/\delta)}\lesssim\mathcal{U}^{\star}(\mu)\hskip 17.00024pt\text{on }\mathcal{E}.

Since ℙ⁡(ℰ)=1\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E})=1, the desired result follows.

Finally, the above bound implies τ<∞\tau<\infty on ℰ\mathcal{E}, hence ℙ⁡(τ<∞)=1\mathbb{P}(\tau<\infty)=1. ∎

19 Real Experiment Details

We evaluate our method on four task types spanning counting, lexical reconstruction, character-level extraction, and basic arithmetic.

  • •

    Object Counting requires the model to identify all items belonging to a target category from a mixed list and return the correct count, thereby testing selective counting and category filtering.

  • •

    Word Unscrambling asks the model to recover the original English word from a scrambled sequence of letters, evaluating lexical knowledge and character-level reordering ability.

  • •

    Second Word Letter is a simple character extraction task from the Instruction-Induction benchmark; in our dataset, each example consists of a single English word, and the model must output its second letter.

  • •

    Sum is a basic arithmetic task in which the input contains two integers and the model is asked to return their sum, providing a controlled setting for deterministic numerical reasoning.

Examples from the dataset are shown below:

  • •

    Object Counting

    • –
      Question: “I have a pig, two ducks, and a dog. How many animals do I have?”
      Answer: “four”
    • –
      Question: “I have a snake, a rabbit, two clarinets, a drum, a flute, and an accordion.
      How many musical instruments do I have?”
      Answer: “five”
  • •

    Word Unscrambling

    • –
      Question: “The word ceahb is a scrambled version of the English word”
      Answer: beach
    • –
      Question: “The word iasso is a scrambled version of the English word”
      Answer: oasis
  • •

    Second Word Letter

    • –
      Question: government
      Answer: o
    • –
      Question: apple
      Answer: p
  • •

    Sum

    • –
      Question: 12 29
      Answer: 41
    • –
      Question: 38 57
      Answer: 95
